utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-96-21-Tbis-R117, the Prosecutor versus Zdravko Mucic, Hazim Delic, Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. My name is James Stewart representing the Prosecutor. I'm assisted today by Gina Butler. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Tom Kuzmanovic and Howard Morrison here on behalf of Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We represent Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Good morning. I am Cynthia Sinatra, and along with Professor Peter Murphy, we're here representing Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a hearing to consider what adjustment should be made to sentences originally passed on these three accused in the light of the Appeals Chamber judgement of the 20th of February of this year. Three matters arise for consideration by the Trial Chamber as remitted to it by the Appeals Chamber: First, to consider what adjustment, if any, should be made to the sentence imposed on Hazim Delic as a result of the quashing of his convictions on counts 1 and 2; second, to impose an appropriate revised sentence on Zdravko Mucic as a result of the Appeal Chamber's finding that the original sentence imposed on him was manifestly inadequate, and to consider what effect, if any, the original Trial Chamber's error in making adverse reference to the failure of the accused to give evidence had on the sentence imposed on him; third, to consider what adjustment, if any, should be made to the original sentences passed on all three accused as a result of the dismissal of the cumulative convictions under Article 3. The Trial Chamber has already identified these as the issues for argument and has received briefs and responses from all parties on them. For that reason, there being no reason to rehearse arguments already put in writing, the Trial Chamber has limited submissions to 45 minutes for each party, the Prosecution to go first. Mr. Stewart, it's for you to begin. I should add that we will take a break as normal at around 11.00. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. I will outline my plan of argument for you to make it simple for you to follow and then deal with the issues. I propose to deal first with the common issue, if I may call it that; namely, the effect of the dismissal of the cumulative convictions. This affects all of the convicted persons. It's also the only issue affecting Landzo. So first I'll deal with that issue. Secondly, I will deal with the effect on Delic's sentence of the quashing of his convictions in relation to one of the killings for which he was originally found criminally responsible. Thirdly, I will deal with the issues relating to the sentence of Mucic. I will then conclude by stating in summary the Prosecutor's submission on what the sentence in each case should be. Let me deal, then, with the effect of the dismissal of the cumulative convictions. The Appeals Chamber quashed the convictions of Mucic, Delic, and Landzo where there was more than one conviction imposed on the basis of the same facts; therefore, the convictions for grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions were maintained, but the convictions for violations of the laws or customs of war, based on the same facts, were quashed. Now, the Appeals Chamber itself could have dealt with the effect of this on the sentences except that it had not been able to hear the parties on that issue. It could not reconstitute itself in order to hear the parties, and in any event, it preferred that a Trial Chamber deal with the issue, because this would preserve the right of further appeal. The Appeals Chamber, however, did deal with all the other issues relating to sentence, whether they were alleged errors in the exercise of discretion or other errors of law, so that this Trial Chamber would be in a position to consider what, if any, adjustment should be made to what the Appeals Chamber considered would otherwise have been appropriate sentences. The question, therefore, as you have defined it, Mr. President, is what adjustment, if any, should be made to the sentences given the dismissal of the cumulative convictions, and I submit that the question is open. If the Trial Chamber takes the view that there should be some reduction in sentence, the Appeals Chamber has recognised that any such adjustment may not necessarily be a substantial one, and I would refer you to the Appeals Chamber's judgement at paragraph 854, page 305, footnote 1458. The Appeals Chamber has also recognised that no adjustment downwards in the sentences imposed may be necessary. And I would refer once again to the judgement at paragraph 769, page 274. And this, of course, is the Prosecutor's position, that there should be no adjustment downwards in the sentences imposed. However, the matter is one for your discretion. The reason why the Prosecutor submits that no downward adjustment to the sentences should be made are as follows: The original Trial Chamber, in our submission, clearly intended to avoid inflicting multiple punishments in this case by imposing concurrent sentences. In effect, the original Trial Chamber imposed a global sentence to reflect the totality of the criminal conduct and overall culpability of the offender. The original Trial Chamber's approach is evident, in our submission, from what it said in paragraph 1286, at page 450 of its judgement, where it noted that it had denied a challenge to cumulative charging earlier in the proceedings on the basis that the issue was only relevant to penalty in the event there were cumulative convictions. It was in this context that the original Trial Chamber said it was imposing concurrent and not consecutive sentences. In taking this approach, the original Trial Chamber was following the practice of some Trial Chambers at this Tribunal and at the Rwanda Tribunal to deal with potential issues of unfairness in connection with cumulative convictions at the sentencing phase. What the original Trial Chamber said it was doing was picked up by the Appeals Chamber, which stated that this Trial Chamber would "... no doubt consider whether the remarks of the original Trial Chamber indicate that there should be no adjustment downwards in the sentences imposed." And that passage that I've just mentioned is to be found in the Appeals Chamber's judgement at paragraph 769, page 274. And that, in a nutshell, is the position that the Prosecutor takes, and that's the basis for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was the, as I recollect, the position of the Trial Chamber in the first case before this Tribunal, Tadic, that concurrent sentences would be passed in relation to Article 3 offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do I recollect correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was that Trial Chamber which dealt originally with the question of cumulative convictions --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- and said it was proper, appropriate to deal with it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The sentencing stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's right. So the Trial Chamber in this case, of course, was following a similar approach. And the approach that should be taken, of course, has now been made very clear by the Appeals Chamber. I'm simply dealing with how the original Trial Chamber in this case was approaching, and it did so on the basis of a practice that was developing both here and in Arusha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, in my submission, making no downward adjustment to the sentences, notwithstanding the dismissal of the cumulative convictions, is a fair approach because while the effect of the Appeals Chamber's decision is to remove the stigma of the cumulative convictions and remove any potential prejudice in the timing of ultimate release from prison if such prejudice should, in fact, arise due to multiple convictions, still the underlying criminal conduct remains the same. So that in a sense, the stigma's been removed, potential prejudice has been removed, but Chamber still has to deal with a constant underlying conduct, and this is what has to be punished, and it is what was punished in the original case. The Appeals Chamber has upheld convictions for extremely serious offences. The conduct of the convicted persons was evil. It involved the taking of life and the infliction of real suffering in the most brutal and callous manner on defenseless victims. The Appeals Chamber found that the sentences would otherwise have been appropriate except in the case of Mucic, where they found that the sentence should be increased. So in the circumstances, I submit, no downward adjustment of any of the sentences is justified simply due to the dismissal of the cumulative convictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suppose the question we have to consider is whether the convictions which were quashed, that is, the convictions for the international offences, adds anything to the seriousness of the criminal conduct, because it's the criminal conduct which essentially we have to punish, not how it's characterised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct. It's the criminal conduct which I am relying upon as meriting a severe sentence, and it has been legally characterised, as a result of the Appeals Chamber's decision, as breaches of the Geneva Conventions. That's very much the position that the Prosecutor is taking. Now, as the Chamber is well aware, that's the only issue which affects Landzo, and therefore I would conclude with respect to him by submitting to you that his sentence of 15 years should be maintained. And the submissions that I've just made I would ask you to take into account in relation to the other two convicted persons, and I'm going to deal with the particular issues that affect each one of them now and I'm not going to say anything more about cumulative convictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you move on, we ought to consider the position in regard to Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. In the case of Landzo, just to summarise very briefly, he killed three detainees in brutal beatings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He was a guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, he was a guard. He was a guard. He tortured three other detainees, which constituted cruel conduct. He caused great suffering to two other detainees. One of them died, but it was not proven that he was directly responsible for that. And he contributed to an atmosphere of terror, causing great suffering to other detainees. He, of course, offered certain factors in mitigation, including his youth and his personality defects; however, the original Trial Chamber took those into account and the Appeals Chamber found that the sentence imposed was within the range, and the only issue was this one that we've just been dealing with. And for that reason, I submit, based on the submissions I've just given you, that the 15-year sentence ought to be maintained. I will return to his sentence in a moment in relation to whether or not there should be a single sentence as opposed to concurrent sentences, but that, I'll deal with in just a very short while. But in terms of the 15-year sentence, which was the top sentence he got, I would submit that that should be maintained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He was sentenced to 15 years for offences involving murder and some involving torture; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. I've detailed them in my written submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If I may, then, Mr. President, I'll deal with Delic next. He received concurrent sentences of 20 years for two wilful killings, but the Appeals Chamber quashed his convictions for one of the killings as being unreasonable. The Appeals Chamber did not, however, overturn the original Trial Chamber's finding that Delic had participated in the brutal beating of the victim, who ultimately died, and I would submit that this is important. So what happened is that the deceased suffered two horrible beatings. The second one resulted in his death. Delic participated in the first, but there was no evidence to prove he had participated in the second fatal assault. The wilful killing where Delic's conviction was upheld was a particularly brutal one. It involved Delic in beating another man to death. So Delic was convicted as well of other serious offences involving horrible brutality, and these were upheld on appeal. If we look at his underlying conduct, he killed one detainee; he tortured and raped two detainees; he engaged in inhumane acts involving the use of an electrical device; he caused great suffering to another detainee, who later died, although he wasn't found directly responsible for that; and he participated in the creation of inhuman living conditions at the camp. In the words of the original Trial Chamber, as I believe they were picked up by the Appeals Chamber - and I would refer you to paragraph 5.18 of the Appeals Chamber's judgement, page 175 - Delic was a direct participant and primary actor in acts of inherent cruelty. In my submission, the totality of his criminal conduct must be weighed, and there is no question of assigning a particular value to a human life by attempting some crude calculation of its worth in terms of years of imprisonment that must be served by the person who took it away. Sentencing is governed by the Statute and the Rules of the Tribunal, and the basic principles in a case such as his are these: The gravity of the offence is the primary consideration in imposing sentence. The governing criterion of sentencing is that it must accurately recognise the gravity of the offences and must reflect the totality of the accused's criminal conduct. Here the totality of the criminal conduct of Delic has been reduced for sentencing purposes, it's true, but the gravity of his offences and the totality of his criminal conduct still merit a severe sentence. I would simply refer to two cases in passing, and I recognise that they present perhaps a different context and are different to a degree, but it is interesting to note the approach that the Appeals Chamber has taken in relation to the issue of adjustment of sentence. In Jelisic, the Appeals Chamber did not change the sentence of 40 years for offences, including 12 murders, even though the Trial Chamber had taken into account an additional murder in fixing that sentence for which the appellant had not been convicted. In Akayesu, the Appeals Chamber did not adjust a life sentence for offences including genocide, of course, where an act of torture was included by the Trial Chamber in the weighing of sentence in error. Now, I'm not putting a great deal of reliance on those cases; I'm simply offering them in support of the submission that the Appeals Chamber appears to favour a global approach to sentence. And it's that sort of approach that I submit ought to apply here. So that the fact that Delic was involved in killing is itself extremely serious, and the sentence must serve to deter others from killing in similar circumstances and it must take into account the principles I've just alluded to. So that I would submit that if there is any downward adjustment to the sentence of 20 years that Delic is now serving, it should be a slight adjustment. I've said in my written material that it could be less than 20, but it certainly should be more than the 15 submitted by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you move from him, his position at the camp I have noted as the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So he had a position of authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the Appeals Chamber has said, and Chambers have said constantly, that the fact that an accused has a position of authority is a factor which is to be taken into consideration when passing sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. And I certainly rely on that. I've dealt, then, with Delic, Mr. President, and if I may, I'll go right to the sentence of Mucic. Two issues arise in relation to that in addition to the one that we've already dealt with in terms of cumulative convictions, and those issues arise in this context: As the Chamber knows, the Prosecutor successfully appealed the seven-year sentence that was imposed on Mucic, which he is now serving. The Appeals Chamber has indicated in so many words that it would have imposed a heavier sentence of around ten years upon him, taking into account factors such as the double jeopardy element inherent in resentencing. The question really, then, is: Does the dismissal of the cumulative convictions in this case, or ought that dismissal pull down the ten-year sentence which the Appeals Chamber would have imposed? And my submission, for reasons already given, is no. And the other question is whether the original Trial Chamber's error in making adverse reference at the time of sentencing to the failure of Mucic to testify should now curtail the sentence of ten years. And once again, my submission is no. Sentencing is not a matter of assigning particular periods of time to particular sentencing factors, but rather a process of making an overall assessment of the circumstances of the case so as to impose an appropriate sentence that takes account of all of the relevant factors. And I'm relying for that proposition on the judgement of the Appeals Chamber at paragraph 841, pages 300 to 301. So while there may have been an error, as the Appeals Chamber has said, it is not such that in light of all the factors that the Appeals Chamber took into account in deciding that the sentence should be increased, a reduction in sentence is warranted. In my submission, there is no reason to depart from the sentence judged appropriate by the Appeals Chamber, and therefore, I would submit that Mucic should receive a sentence of ten years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He was the commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He was the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He was convicted as a superior, and the matters we have to deal with are, in all but one case, offences committed as a superior, but they involve wilful killing of a number detainees, torture of others, wilfully causing great suffering, inhuman treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He was, as superior responsible in relation to the wilful killing of nine people, the torture of six, the causing of great suffering to three, the inhuman treatment of six others, and, of course, causing great suffering by virtue of the inhumane conditions of the camp. Now, he was responsible, as commander, for those conditions, so that he certainly, in the view of the Appeals Chamber, deserved a higher sentence than he got at the original trial. And my submission, as you know, as you've heard, is that nothing that has happened in relation to the other issues that affect him ought to reduce that ten-year sentence. The only other point that I wanted to raise, Mr. President, was the one relating to the imposition of a single sentence reflecting the totality of the criminal conduct of Mucic, and that's in the application of Rule 87(C). Certainly the Prosecutor would support such an approach, and I would submit that it is open to you to take a similar approach in relation to the sentences of Delic and Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, your submission, then, is that the adverse reference by the Trial Chamber to the failure of the accused to testify is not the kind of factor that would have influenced the sentence and should not be taken into account. You place emphasis on the global approach to sentencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But in a sense, I'm approaching that issue from the point of view of the Appeals Chamber in the sense that the Appeals Chamber took a look at a number of factors and found that those factors ought to have resulted in a higher sentence than seven years, and my submission is that that's so. And if you add the negative factor that we've just been talking about, this error in reference to his failure to testify, which should not have been made and should not have been taken into account, even if you add that negative factor, it's not of sufficient weight to pull down a sentence of around ten years. In other words, it doesn't have an impact on what this Trial Chamber should do in the wake of the Appeals Chamber's judgement. It's a slightly different approach than simply saying that it didn't have any effect on the sentence that the original Trial Chamber imposed. It's impossible to say. In fact, even the Appeals Chamber couldn't really say. They say it may have had affect and the fact that it could have is sufficient to raise it as an issue before you. But the original Trial Chamber, even if they took that into account as a negative factor, only gave Mucic seven years, which was manifestly inadequate in the view of the Appeals Chamber. And my submission to you was that when you come to deal with the issues that you have to now, the principal one being the dismissal of the cumulative convictions, it's simply not a factor of sufficient weight to detract from the ten-year sentence. That's the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The concern that I have about the global approach to sentence is that, and you have relied on it on several occasion this is morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- is that it might be difficult, if that is taken to its logical conclusion, to ever identify a single factor as having an effect on that global sentence, because conceivably there must be -- it must be possible to identify factors that could reduce a global sentence. And I'm a little concerned that the way you're developing your argument might lead to the conclusion that it would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to have identified a single factor or factors that could properly pull down and reduce a global sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because a global sentence, by definition, is already a sentence that takes account of a wide range of factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I would submit that to some degree it's difficult to treat this issue in the abstract, and my submission to you is a very concrete one. It's simply that in this sentencing circumstance, this particular factor doesn't result in a reduction of what would otherwise be the appropriate sentence of ten years. However, if the Trial Chamber -- a Trial Chamber whose sentence was being reviewed by an Appeals Chamber had articulated factors, it ought to be possible, as in fact happened in this case, for the Appeals Chamber to identify factors upon which undue emphasis has perhaps been placed. If, for example, a Trial Chamber put too much emphasis on the issue of mitigation, on mitigating factors, this is something that ought to be able to be identified by the parties and by the Appeals Chamber, or if too great emphasis was placed on deterrence or retribution as general factors or if particular features of the case were characterised in a certain way and thus given weight. Clearly in the reasons of the Trial Chamber, it ought to be possible to identify them if there is an error and to correct the error by a downward adjustment. There is always going to be an element of discretion both in the evaluation of the factors on appellate review and in what to do to correct the situation. That's inescapable, but I would submit, Your Honour, that it's not impossible at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just to conclude the point I was making about the single sentence reflecting the totality of the criminal conduct, the Prosecutor supports such an approach here because we take the position that this is really what the Trial Chamber originally was trying to achieve, and it works justice in the case because it takes into account the gravity of the offences and the underlying criminal conduct. To sum up then, however the sentences are structured, the Prosecutor submits that Mucic should receive a sentence of no less than ten years, Delic should have a sentence close to 20 years - the exact sentence being a matter for you - and Landzo's sentence of 15 years should be maintained. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We turn to the Defence. Mr. Kuzmanovic, are you going first?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Mr. Morrison and I will be splitting our argument, and we will not take the 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. And you're addressing us, of course, on behalf of Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first thing I would like to advise the Court is obviously we are not going to be reiterating things we've written in our brief. I think the Court is well aware and has read our submissions, and we will not be repeating them in our oral submissions. I will state, though, however, that at least as far as the issue of the adverse reference that we've discussed to Mr. Mucic failing to testify, the Prosecution, in its brief, has not really provided the Court with any authority or any persuasive argument as to why that adverse reference should not be used to pull down Mr. Mucic's sentence, and I will refer to my arguments in our brief in that regard. I would like to direct the Court to paragraph 787 of the Appeals Chamber's decision. In that section of the decision, the Appeals Chamber said that: "It is essential --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down, particularly if he's reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are asked to slow down. Remember the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Particularly if you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. "It is essential that the sentencing Judge is in possession of the fullest information possible concerning the defendant's life and characteristics." And I submit that the Appeals Chamber has put this Trial Chamber in a difficult situation, because it can't be said that this new Trial Chamber is really in possession of this information. And unless this new Trial Chamber has had the ability to view the videotape, review the transcripts, the thousands of pages of transcripts, I submit that it can't be in possession of the fullest information possible in order to deal with the sentencing issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, you know the position. It's been remitted to us by the Appeals Chamber with certain instructions which we propose to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, but my submission is that in order to get a full picture of who our client is, I don't think under the Appeals Chamber's guidance that the new Trial Chamber has that possibility without reviewing the things that I have discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we have followed the instructions given to us, and that is the approach which we shall continue to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I understand that, and that's why I would suggest to the Court to review closely the original Trial Chamber's judgement, because in the original Trial Chamber's judgement, at paragraph 1240, the Court specifically said and I quote: "It is significant to observe that Mr. Mucic has not been found guilty of actively participating in any of the offences charged in the indictment. All of the convictions are in respect of offences for which he was culpable and liable because of criminal acts by subordinates." And that gets us to the big picture when you look at Mr. Mucic as an individual. What did he have to do with anything, with the arrest of people brought to Celebici? What position of military authority, if any, did he have there? What credible evidence existed that he was the commanding officer before the end of July of 1992? And I think those are all things that we've discussed both at the Trial Chamber level and at the Appeals Chamber level. The other issue which I would refer the Court to is the standard of review that we argued in our brief at pages 19 to 20 on what the Court should do on issues of sentencing. It's our position that the Court should follow a similar standard to Aleksovski on the issue of reasonableness and deference to a court on the -- the Aleksovski case dealt with reasonableness and deference to a Trial Chamber on the issue of factual determinations. It's our position that this Trial Chamber should make that same deference to the Trial Court on the issue of sentencing determinations. I would like to leave the Court before I hand this matter over to Mr. Morrison with the following thought: What other case have we had testimony in which a detainee victim at a camp has said that if 20 per cent of the people were like Mr. Mucic, there would not have been any war in Bosnia? I shun to think that if we would have had 20 per cent of the people in Bosnia that were Todorovics or Jelisics, I shun to think what would have happened in Bosnia. I think the fact that the Trial Chamber made that initial review of the record and that we've had testimony on Mr. Mucic's behalf from a victim, that tells you the difficulty that the Trial Chamber had initially in coming to its decision on sentencing. If Mr. Mucic was this person who was this horrible camp commander, we would not have had a sentence of seven years; we would have had a sentence of 20 years, 25 years, even Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. more. And I think what you can see is the Trial Chamber's grappling with the factual issues in the case and the difficulties it had in coming to its conclusion and issuing a sentence of seven years, based on the fact that it felt that Mr. Mucic's failings were not that of someone who had malice, and I think that's a very important determination that the Trial Chamber made that this Court should look closely at. I will now turn the matter over to Mr. Morrison. Thank you, Your Honours. Unless there are any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: If it please Your Honours. There's really three matters I would like to address your minds to in respect of this exercise, and the first is this: Of course Mucic was held to be the camp commander, but it's the position of authority that convicted him, not that sentenced him. And I go back to what my learned friend Mr. Kuzmanovic has said in respect of that: When one looks at the underlying character of the person, one really does have to go back to what the Trial Chamber analysed and what they determined, and it is remarkable that a detainee in those circumstances should have been able to say that which he did. And he wasn't the only detainee, as Your Honours will see from the trial transcript when you read that portion of it. At paragraph 853 of the judgement of the Appeals Chamber, they say this: They take account of the various considerations relating to the gravity of Mr. Mucic's offences and the aggravating circumstances; therefore, they've taken account of everything which my learned friend Mr. Stewart was advocated, as well as the mitigating circumstances referred to by the Trial Chamber. They also take into account double jeopardy element involved in resentencing. Of course, the double jeopardy element is really an element which goes to the mind of the defendant or detainee as to how he perceives his sentence, because it's his jeopardy and it's nobody else's. And in doing that, they say they would have imposed on Mr. Mucic a heavier sentence of around ten years' imprisonment. That is, with great respect, imprecise. It can only sensibly and practicably mean a sentence of between 9 and 11 years. It's difficult to imagine another or better, in my respectful submission, definition of "around ten years."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's leaving the matter to the discretion of this Trial Chamber but giving it an indication of the sort of sentence they had in mind. The difficulty about the submission that you and Mr. Kuzmanovic have made is that all these factors have been taken into consideration, firstly by the Trial Chamber in imposing what for a camp commander would appear to be a low sentence of seven years, and the Appeals Chamber in ordering or deciding that it was too low and recommending about ten years. Why should we not follow that indication?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, let me deal with it from this standpoint, then: Supposing I simply concede for the purposes of this argument that that should be the approach, which, with respect, I do, for the purposes of this argument. We then analyse what "around ten years" means, and we look at it from the point of view of the defendant, who is the person who is going to be the subject of the sentence. Because that's part of the double jeopardy argument, the most central issue in double jeopardy, is the effect upon the defendant of a resentencing exercise. And if one looks at it from that point of view and says, "What is the practical effect of around ten years' imprisonment?" in my submission, the common-sense interpretation is something between 9 and 11 years. Now, if one looks at that and sees the ambiguity in that, 2 years between 9 and 11 is a substantial period of time. And where there is an ambiguity in law, the general principle is that the ambiguities are resolved in favour of those who would be in jeopardy if they were otherwise resolved. So let's look at it from that point of view and suggest that therefore, in equity, around ten years' imprisonment would mean the lower end of that ambiguity, nine years. One then looks afresh at the cumulative sentencing. And in my respectful submission, it would be disingenuous to suppose - because the Trial Chamber did not set out in specific detail how it approached that element of sentencing - it would be disingenuous to suppose that they didn't take some account in sentencing of the cumulative convictions, and the danger is, therefore, that they did, and that also goes to double jeopardy. But more importantly in respect to Mr. Mucic, in my submission, is the error by the Trial Chamber in referring to the failure of Mr. Mucic to give evidence. That's been treated, and understandably, but it's been treated dismissally by the Prosecution in this case. In my respectful submission, it's a matter which is of considerable moment in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, that a Trial Chamber should have made what is - and one has to put it bluntly - a fundamental error. It's about as fundamental as it gets. There are many jurisdictions in which, if such an error was made during the course of a judicial process and it came to light before that person was convicted or sentenced, the conviction would be swept aside and a retrial ordered. Certainly, of course, in my own jurisdiction, if a judge summed the case up to the jury making that sort of error by suggesting to the jury that they could take into account a failure to give evidence, we would know what the consequences would be. This is not a small matter. The trouble is, we do not know, even allowing for the seven-year original sentence, exactly what proportion of that sentence was taken into account by the Trial Chamber in the wrongful prejudice that was given to the failure to give evidence. If they didn't take it into account at all, my submission is that they would have said so, because it is something which was so fundamental. We don't know. We can only assume. And the assumption, in my submission, has to be in favour of the defendant. They must have held it against him, in broad practical terms. It is impossible to define what proportion of the sentence was affected by that, but that it was some, in my submission, is of such great moment and of such great danger that it cannot be ignored. And this Chamber, in my submission, should give effect to what the Appeals Chamber has said as to that, as to the error, by giving a reduction from that nine-year basis, which, in my submission, would be the equitable way of approaching this case. That's, of course, a matter for discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Morrison, what we have to consider, surely, is this: Is this sentence, aside from this remark, a proper sentence or not? Because, as you rightly say, we cannot go back and see what was in the minds of the original Trial Chamber. We have to put ourselves or ask ourselves: Is this a sentence which is proper, or is it one which has been affected by this comment? And we've got to judge the matter, as far as we can, objectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course. The best evidence we have of what was in the minds of the Trial Chamber is in their judgement. Indeed, the only evidence we have of what was in the minds of the Trial Chamber was in their judgement. And we know that part of what was in their minds was the fact that Mr. Mucic had failed to give evidence. And that is a balancing exercise, of course, for Your Honours to consider. I pose the alternative proposition. Imagine if the Trial Chamber had actively said, "Well, we're going to reduce the sentences where people give evidence, whether they're convicted or not." There would be a howl of protest from the Prosecution that the jurisprudence of the Tribunal was being perverted by things which should not have been taken into account. Well, this is simply the other side of the coin. It's the overall aim of the Security Council and the setting up of this Tribunal to present to the world a Tribunal where the fundamental principles of law are not only upheld but honed and perfected. And in making the sort of determination the Trial Chamber did, they fell -- with respect, fall short of that, and this is an opportunity for this Trial Chamber to amend that error. Your Honour, unless there's anything else I can usefully deal with ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. Yes. Who is next? Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll go next. May it please the Court. The issues have been fully briefed on both sides. In fact, I think the Trial Chamber may think I briefed it a little too fully, so I'm not going to repeat what's in the briefs. What I propose to do is answer a few questions that I think have been raised; second, present some kind of what I think is a logical way to deal with the issues that are presented before you; and third, to discuss this case in a little bit of length based on this Trial Chamber's analysis in Todorovic. The first thing I want to do is, there were two questions that were asked by the Bench. Judge May, you mentioned to the Prosecutor about an aggravation based on a position of authority, that that's a factor that can be considered. Your Honour, let me suggest to you this: In Todorovic, you did that. You also held that an aggravating factor must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. Now, I could be wrong on this, but as I recall, in every case where superior authority has been a factor in aggravation, that person had either been held liable on a command responsibility theory, superior responsibility theory, or could have been. For instance, in Todorovic, he could have been held responsible on a command responsibility theory. He was not. But you clearly said in the judgement that he was the chief of police and that put him into that position. Here Mr. Delic has been acquitted of all command responsibility counts and allegations. The Prosecutor appealed that, and the acquittals were affirmed. Therefore, you cannot show beyond a reasonable doubt that he had superior authority. And under your holding in Todorovic that an aggravating factor must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt, I would suggest to you that you should not take Mr. Delic's status as deputy camp Commander into account in assessing punishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He was convicted under Article 7(1).

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He was convicted of what he did, not on a derivative responsibility theory like Article 7(3).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what he was convicted of, on the other hand, was the wilful killing of one detainee, causing suffering or serious injury to another, two counts of torture by way of rape, and another count of inhumane treatment of detainees, and another of causing great suffering. He was convicted -- if you're right about that argument, he was still convicted of obviously very serious offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no one is submitting that they weren't serious offences of conviction, but, Your Honour, you raised that in a question to the Prosecutor, and I thought I should address it. Judge Robinson, you raised the issue of global sentencing. And let me just suggest to you this: Sentencing is not a scientific thing. It's something that Judges have to look into their hearts and their minds, and they try to do as best they can. And in some jurisdictions -- well, I practice in two jurisdictions at home. One is a state court and one is a federal court. In the state court, there is broad discretion in the sentencing authority. It might be 5 to 99 years or life in the penitentiary for a crime, and anywhere within that would be within the sentencing authority's discretion. On the other hand, in my federal courts, there's been an attempt to set up guidelines that are really binding on the judges and to narrow their discretion, and I would just suggest to you, Your Honour, that this Trial Chamber -- and I really haven't -- this Tribunal seems to have picked some kind of a middle ground where it says the Trial Chamber has great discretion in assessing punishment but that it has to explain its reasons for doing so, and that if its reasons show an abuse of discretion, then they're subject to review by an Appeals Chamber. So I think that probably what should be done is that the Trial Chamber will set forth in some detail its reasoning for picking a specific sentence, and that would be how it could be reviewed. With that, Your Honour, let me proceed this way: As far as I know, Mr. Delic is the first person in front of this Tribunal to be remanded for resentencing or an adjustment in sentence based on a reduction in the total amount of criminality, of criminal conduct. Again, I could stand to be corrected, but I believe that is true. The Prosecutor at the Appeals Chamber, the Appeals Chamber itself, and the Prosecutor here all seem to agree that the sentence should reflect the total amount of criminality and that if the total amount of criminal conduct is reduced, the sentence should be reduced, the total sentence, the overall sentence. It's hard to determine, from reading the original Trial Chamber's judgement, how much of the total global sentence assessed against Mr. Delic was based on the facts of the murder of Scepo Gotovac, counts 1 and 2 in the indictment. Clearly, a reading of the Trial Chamber's judgement shows that they were offended by this. It was an old man who was killed based on their findings of a 50-year-old dispute that arose during World War II, purely for revenge, which is a bad motive, and that could not help but affect the original Trial Chamber's decision on what sentence to impose. Unfortunately, they erred, because he was not guilty of that murder. That is why the case is back here. Since this Trial Chamber sees its role - and I don't disagree with you - as adjusting the sentence, I think your analysis has to be to attempt to determine what effect that convictions on counts 1 and 2 had on the total sentence that was assessed, and I think you have to read the Trial Chamber's judgement on sentencing to get a feel for how the original Trial Chamber felt about that offence. At that point, then, I think you should reassess Mr. Delic's sentence by attempting to remove the effect of the improper conviction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moran. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And having done that and having arrived at a sentence, a presumptive sentence for Mr. Delic, then I think it becomes the second part of the analysis to adjust for the cumulative convictions. And again this Trial Chamber is going to, I think, have to try to determine what the original Trial Chamber did and how it was affected by the cumulative convictions. I've cited some cases to the Trial Chamber from American jurisdictions on what we call multiplicious sentencing, and frankly, it's a very difficult thing for an appellate court or a reviewing court to deal with. It is very difficult. But it is clear that even with concurrent sentences, the second conviction does constitute a separate punishment for the crime, if for no other reason that you are labelled as a criminal for two reasons rather than one. And I would suggest to the -- that in that analysis, there should be some reduction in the overall sentence, not just for Mr. Delic but for all of these defendants, simply based on the cumulative convictions. Now, in looking at the sentencing factors I think you should look at directly based on the reduction in the total amount of criminality, that issue's been briefed. Of course, Todorovic came down after that, and so I will just discuss some of the factors the Trial Chamber considered in Todorovic. First, it seems from my reading of the case, and I may have misread it, but I think this Trial Chamber seemed to consider deterrence and retribution almost together, that if the sentence was sufficient for retribution, then it would be sufficient to deter others later from committing the same offence. You looked at the nature of the crimes and the way that the crimes were committed. But although you didn't say it in your judgement, it appeared that you were making sure that you didn't consider both the crime and how it was committed separately from the nature of the crime and seemed to consider those together in arriving at a sentence, so that you wouldn't say, "This person committed a horrible, brutal murder and so the sentence merits X, and it was also horrible and brutal so it merits something on top of X." The Trial Chamber considered them together. Other factors that the Trial Chamber seemed to look at in mitigation were you discussed four factors: guilty plea, cooperation with the Prosecutor, remorse, and diminished mental capacity. Well, of course in this case there were no guilty pleas. My suggestion to the Court on that would be you're correct in Todorovic, that in every jurisdiction that I know, if a person pleads guilty, that's considered a matter in mitigation. But the other side of the coin, the fact that he insists upon his rights to a trial, is not a matter in aggravation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That must be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Cooperation with the Prosecutor. Mr. Delic gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor at the time of his arrest and the time of his initial detention in The Hague. That was introduced into evidence in front of the Trial Chamber. He was not asked to testify against anyone else. He was not asked for anything beyond that statement. Expressed remorse. There is nothing in the record about expressed remorse one way or the other. Diminished mental capacity. There is, in the record from the original Trial Chamber, a report from Dr. Prince from McGill University that Mr. Delic suffers or suffered at the time of the examination from post-traumatic stress syndrome. Now, in Todorovic, there was some question about whether or not he suffered from PTSD, and there was a question about whether or not he suffered from PTSD at the time of the offences on whether it developed later, and, therefore, this Chamber did not consider post-traumatic stress syndrome is matter in mitigation. Frankly, Dr. Prince's report is not clear as to when it developed. I will just refer it to you. It's attached to my sentencing memo from the original Trial Chamber. Issues in mitigation that the Trial Chamber did not discuss in Aleksovski were discussed in our briefs. I think they've been discussed at some length, and unless there's some questions, I will give back whatever remaining time I have to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, we've also got to do this -- you put forward one approach. We've also got to determine what on the facts is a proper sentence, the facts as they're put to us, and we have to determine whether the sentence, as passed, needs adjustment or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, everyone, I think -- well, this Trial Chamber hasn't been asked and hasn't said, but the Prosecution, both at the Appeals Chamber and here, and we have said that based on the appellate acquittal, there should be some reduction in sentence. The dispute is over how much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the words used by the Appeals Chamber were "adjustment, if any," and we're going to have to determine not necessarily whether there should be adjustment, whether there should be adjustment, and if so, how much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is going to be the approach we're going have to adopt, isn't it, rather than trying to start sentencing again and trying to work out what was in the minds of original Trial Chamber, which we cannot determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the two separate approaches, I think, are this: One is resentencing, in which instance the entire range of punishment would be open to this Trial Chamber, and the other is an attempt to correct or adjust based on errors made by the original Trial Chamber. Now, I -- from reading the various orders, scheduling orders, and decisions of the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber's holding, it seems to me it is an adjustment that should be based on the original sentence as opposed to -- on all three defendants, not just on my client, as opposed to a complete resentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you're right about that, then the question is, adjustment -- is any adjustment required? Two stages I should say. Is any adjustment required, and if so, how much? You seem to posit that it's been agreed that there should be an adjustment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I quoted, and I can find it in my original brief, two paragraphs from the Appeals Chamber that talked about sentences reflecting the total amount of criminality, the totality of the criminality. The Prosecutor at the Appeals Chamber talked about the total amount of the criminality and says if there's one crime, each one of which would have merited 20 years, the two of them together might merit 22 to 25 or some other period of imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What you say, in a nutshell, in fact, you've said is that because there has been in this case a quashing of convictions, therefore there's a reduction in criminality, therefore there should be a reduction in sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's what we think the Appeals Chamber said and the totality principle requires, and the question would be: How much? We have suggested that it should be in the neighbourhood of 15 years. But in any case, since the total amount of criminal conduct for which Mr. Delic has been held liable is reduced, it seems to follow almost directly that the total punishment ought to be reduced to fit the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Crimes, plural. Your Honour, neither in the written submissions nor in my oral submissions to this Trial Chamber have I attempted to denigrate or minimise the gravity of the offences of which Mr. Delic stands convicted. I can't do that. He has been convicted of serious offences. But he has been acquitted of a serious offence, a serious offence which the original Trial Chamber found was committed in an especially heinous way, for an especially bad motive, against an especially vulnerable victim, and therefore, I think that there is a substantial reduction in the amount of criminality. Just looking at the motives on the other murder convictions -- the other murder conviction. Excuse me. In that case, the complainant, the deceased, was accused of being a sniper for the Bosnian Serbs. Whether or not he was, I'm not -- that's not, I don't think, relevant. The fact is he was accused of that and the evidence was appeared to believe -- or appeared to show that the people in the camp thought he was guilty about being a sniper. This Tribunal has found, has held, the Office of the Prosecutor had shown in indictments time after time that sniping is considered to be a very, very serious offence. One need only look at General Galic's indictment on the Sarajevo case. So the motives for the two murders I think are different. Now, no one is ever saying, and I'm not going to tell you that I think murder can be a minor offence. There is no misdemeanour murder. But if motive and the way the crime is carried out is to have any weight at sentencing, as you've said in Todorovic it does and as the Appeals Chamber says in other cases, then you have to look at those two murders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think you have to look at those two murders and attempt, as best you can, to see how the count 1 murder affected the judgement and the sentence of the original Trial Chamber. And I'm suggesting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you've made that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It's a very difficult task, and I don't envy you for it. Unless there are some other questions again, I will give some time back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I would suggest, we're ten minutes away from the break time. If the Court would allow us, we would ask to take the break so we're not interrupted in the middle of our argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Good idea. We'll adjourn now for half an hour, which means we will be back at twenty past eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Of course, you're aware that I'm Cynthia Sinatra and this is Peter Murphy, and we're going to be sharing the argument today. I don't think we're going to be very lengthy, because we only have a few -- one basic issue is whether there's any adjustment based on the cumulative convictions that were dismissed. I also want to say that we're really happy to see that Judge Fihri is healthy after last time, and we're also very happy that four of us were able to fly here under the conditions right now and be here with this Court and we didn't have to reset this again. I want to refer back to our brief on the adjustment of sentence. I'm not going to reargue everything. This Trial Chamber is well aware of our arguments put forth. I did want to remind the Court that when you look at the summary that we have on the first and second page of the brief, though, that initially Esad Landzo was charged with 18 convictions. He had 18 convictions. The Trial Court, of course, found that he was not guilty of two, and then under the cumulative sentencing, eight of them were dismissed. So we're only left with eight counts that we're dealing with. Although, I'm not trying to make light of the charges. Mr. Landzo still stands convicted, after the dismissal of the cumulative convictions, of three counts of murder, three counts of torture, and two counts of cruel treatment, which are very serious crimes in this Tribunal. I do want to address Judge May's statement that criminal responsibility also should be -- the aggravating circumstances should take into account command responsibility. As you're aware, Mr. Landzo had no command responsibility at Celebici camp. He was an 18-, 19-year-old guard with no military prior training and, you know, he was just forced to come in and defend his home and city at the moment, so he really had no military standing whatsoever. The Court has already taken into consideration the diminished mental responsibility in mitigation of punishment, but I want to say that as an 18-, 19-year-old at the time in 1992, Mr. Landzo is now 28 years old, and one of the considerations that this Court takes seriously when resentencing or in adjusting right now would be in rehabilitation. And although the Trial Court did consider the certain rehabilitation and psychological therapy that Mr. Landzo had during his confinement, he's now been confined five and a half years, and three years have passed since the first sentencing occurred. It was November of 1998, so we're just one and a half months short of three years, and I'd like to just take this moment to update the Court on some of the progress that Mr. Landzo has made and ask this Court to please consider these mitigating circumstances. These are issues that were already considered by the Trial Court - and I won't go over them - such as his voluntary surrender. He did attempt to cooperate with the Prosecution. And when you compare this to Todorovic, who was really charged with many heinous crimes - because the Prosecution needed his assistance, and the Prosecution didn't need assistance in our case - I don't think that Mr. Landzo should be punished for the fact that the Prosecution didn't need his assistance at that time during the trial. Mr. Landzo testified. He admitted his guilt. He now has learned perfect English. He assists the guards over at the UN Detention Centre in interpreting for some of the other Yugoslav detainees. And he has done all of this on his own. Not only has he taught himself English, he has taught himself computer skills, and he's assisting the other detainees over there with their computer skills. When I first met Mr. Landzo in December of 1996, he had twice attempted to commit suicide. He'd been on hunger strikes. He wrote a letter to the Prosecution asking to be executed by a firing squad. The transformation of Esad Landzo from 1996 to today probably has lot to do with changing from a young boy to a man, a maturation process --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sinatra. We did have some difficulty with the transcript. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. He also is friends with all ethnic groups over there. He's gotten a job while he's in the detention centre. He works in the laundry, and he takes great pride in the work that he does. In fact, all the other detainees ask him to please do their laundry because he's so neat. He's been seeking his faith also, and he says he has no enemies left. And I would like to ask the Court, although I'm not finished with my argument, if the Court would allow Mr. Landzo to address the Court for a few moments in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Ms. Sinatra. We considered applications in relation to addresses by the accused. We're not going to allow it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stewart had said that it's a fair approach that Mr. Landzo receive no adjustment. My question to this Court is: How could it be fair when, of course, under Article 24 this Court takes into consideration all the aggravating and mitigating circumstances and the criminality? When his criminality has been reduced from 18 charges to 8 charges, the fair decision on this Court would be to adjust the sentence proportionately. I'd like to remind this Court also that in the last three years, the jurisprudence of the Tribunal has moved forward in regards to sentencing. We have so many more decisions to rely upon than we did in 1998, and this Court doesn't have to ignore them. I know that Mr. Moran has gone over the Todorovic decision with you, and I don't want to, you know, reread the whole decision, but this Court is well aware of the charges against Mr. Todorovic. Even though he did cooperate with the Prosecution, he also admitted -- showed his remorse, admitted his guilt, just as Mr. Landzo has done, and the Court thought that a fair sentence was ten years. Mr. Stewart says that a fair sentence for Mr. Landzo remains at 15 years. We disagree with this. We would like to also ask the Court not to decide this in a vacuum. Mr. Landzo did not have any command responsibility or any superiority, and if the -- if we have to do comparisons not only with Todorovic, who was a police chief, but also with one of the other accused Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in this trial who was found to have command responsibility and only received seven years, we're asking this Court to make sure that Esad Landzo's sentence is not any more than seven years also. In fact, I'm going to give all this time back to Mr. Murphy right now unless this Court has any questions of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: May it please the Court. I will be very brief indeed. The Court knows that we filed a motion drawing the attention of the Court to an issue of jurisdiction, and I appreciate the Court has denied that motion, and it is not my intention to try to reopen it. It is, however, my intention to suggest that -- and perhaps the wording of the motion was not entirely fortunate since we put it in terms of the jurisdiction of the Appeals Chamber. There is, of course, an issue as to the jurisdiction of this Chamber, and I simply re-urge the matters of law that were contained in the motion in that regard. I think, Your Honours, in the way in which this issue arose at a very late stage is really significant, that we, as a group of Defence counsel, were trying to articulate what we saw as a problem of the difference between an adjustment of sentence and a resentencing. And in the course of exploring that, we asked ourselves the question, well, what is the law which gives a Trial Chamber the jurisdiction to sentence in this Tribunal? And when we looked at that question, it became clear, to us at least, that the Statute of the Tribunal and the Rules give the Trial Chambers, the Appeals Chamber very specific powers, very specific jurisdiction, which it seemed to us did not cover the present case. We brought it to the attention of the Trial Chamber because it seemed to us to be an issue of some importance which, if not resolved in this case, will inevitably have to be resolved at some later time or in another case. The issue, Your Honours, if I may say so, was really framed, I think, during the course of argument this morning when, in response to a question from Mr. Moran, Judge May made the statement, I think, that we have to determine what the proper sentence is, the proper adjustment. My submission is that it is not really practicable to make an adjustment of sentence without an understanding of the underlying criminality, and that's really the issue implicit in the Court's task, because when one -- if it were just a question of, well, we had a certain number of crimes of which they'd been convicted originally, today we have less crimes, then of course it would be a very simple issue as to whether that really makes any difference. In order to exercise discretion properly, the Trial Chamber really has to go back and look a little bit at the overall criminality, and that really means looking at the record in much the way the first Trial Chamber would have looked at it. And that's really the dilemma that the Appeals Chamber has - with all great respect to the Appeals Chamber - has created for this Trial Chamber. How do we make a proper adjustment without a understanding of the criminality? And if we explore the criminality, how do we do that without looking at the record and trying to reconstruct, as it were, what the first Trial Chamber had in mind? Your Honours, it may be for that reason and for whatever reason, however, that the Trial Chamber, even on an issue of adjustment, I would submit, that what the Trial Chamber is doing is a form of resentencing. It may not be resentencing in the name way, in which one would perhaps in England, for example, when after receiving certain reports one might go back and look at sentence again, but it is, nonetheless, a resentencing. And if it is a resentencing, then the Trial Chamber is bound by the Statute and by the Rules, and Article 4 and Rule 101(B), taken together, make it mandatory for the Trial Chamber to consider all the matters enumerated in Article 24, which, as the Court knows, involve not only the circumstances of the crimes themselves but also the circumstances of the offenders. It was for that reason that we felt it appropriate to make our motion, to give the Court a chance to rule on that and to say that perhaps the motion filed on behalf of Delic, while not couched in exactly the same terms, must have had a great deal of merit insofar as it suggested that the whole picture should be looked at. I would also say, Your Honours, perhaps that clearly one thing that the Appeals Chamber had in mind was that by -- by remitting the case to a new Trial Chamber, it would preserve the right of appeal. But an interesting question was what right of appeal really would be involved in simply a question of yes or no on the question of do we adjust or not. Clearly, if there were to be a substantive right of appeal, we would have to look at the propriety of the sentences, not only just in terms of the Appeals Chamber's ruling, but how does that reflect the criminality in the circumstances of the accused as it appears from the entire record? So I suggest, Your Honour, that this Trial Chamber is to some extent in a dilemma not of its own making, and even though it may not be appropriate for it to pass judgement on the Appeals Chamber's jurisdiction, it is certainly appropriate for it to pass judgement on its own jurisdiction. And I would respectfully suggest that that's almost inevitable in the circumstances of this case. Unless the Court has any questions, Your Honour, I don't believe I have any more submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will consider these matters. We will not be in a position to pass sentence today. We will reflect on them, and we will pass sentence on a date of which the parties will be notified. The Court will rise.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.46 a.m.
